Eminent

EM-ih-nent — starts like 'emperor'; an eminent person stands out like royalty in their field. Note: eminent (famous) is easy to mix up with imminent (about to happen) — they look and sound alike but mean very different things. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Eminent is famous and respected within a particular field or profession.

An eminent panel of judges, each a leader in their field, was invited to evaluate the science fair finalists.

Worked Example

A researcher spends forty years studying a rare disease, publishes hundreds of papers, trains dozens of doctors around the world, and is eventually asked to advise the World Health Organization on how to respond to future outbreaks.

Being so respected and well-known within your field that world organizations seek your advice is exactly what eminent means. Unlike 'famous,' which can apply to anyone widely known, eminent specifically implies deep respect earned through real accomplishment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distinguished: honored and respected for achievement

renowned: widely known and admired

illustrious: famous, especially for great achievements

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unknown: not known or recognized by others

obscure: not well known; hard to notice

Where it sits · how large the reputation has grown — notable → eminent → legendary

notable vs. eminent: Notable is weaker than eminent — something notable is simply worth mentioning, while eminent describes someone widely and deeply respected within their field.

legendary vs. eminent: Legendary can feel even bigger than eminent: eminent describes real, earned respect, but legendary suggests a reputation so large it borders on myth.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e- (ex-)

prefix — e- (ex-): out (Latin)

root — -min-

root — -min-: to project, to jut out (Latin (eminere))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin eminere combined e- ('out') with a root meaning 'to project or jut,' and the suffix -ent turns it into an adjective -- 'jutting out.' Someone eminent literally stands out from the crowd, which is why the word means famous and respected.

Use the root in a new word: prominent

Use the root in a new word: prominent: The senator's portrait hung in a prominent spot at the entrance of the museum.
